Primer 6 measured disease in one group. Now we compare 2 groups, which is where
analytical epidemiology starts.

## The 2×2 table

4 numbers. Learn this layout and keep to it. Many mistakes with odds ratios are
really mistakes about which cell is which.

<table class="twobytwo">
<tr><th></th><th>Disease</th><th>No disease</th><th>Total</th></tr>
<tr><th>Exposed</th><td>a</td><td>b</td><td>a + b</td></tr>
<tr><th>Unexposed</th><td>c</td><td>d</td><td>c + d</td></tr>
</table>

Exposure down the side, outcome across the top. Always.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
In the code below the four cells are called `a`, `b`, `cc` and `d`. The third is
`cc` rather than `c` because `c()` is one of R's most-used functions, and naming
a variable over it is a habit that will bite you later.
:::

Our worked example: a cohort of 2,000 adults followed for five years for
coronary heart disease.

<table class="twobytwo">
<tr><th></th><th>CHD</th><th>No CHD</th><th>Total</th></tr>
<tr><th>Smoker</th><td>90</td><td>910</td><td>1000</td></tr>
<tr><th>Non-smoker</th><td>30</td><td>970</td><td>1000</td></tr>
</table>

```{webr}
a  <- 90    # exposed,   disease
b  <- 910   # exposed,   no disease
cc <- 30    # unexposed, disease   (named cc, because c() is a function)
d  <- 970   # unexposed, no disease

# Risk in each group
risk_exposed   <- a / (a + b)
risk_unexposed <- cc / (cc + d)

risk_exposed
risk_unexposed
```

Risk is **0.09 in smokers** and **0.03 in non-smokers**. Everything below is a
different way of comparing those two numbers.

## Risk ratio — how many times more likely

$$\text{RR} = \frac{\text{risk in the exposed}}{\text{risk in the unexposed}}$$

```{webr}
a <- 90; b <- 910; cc <- 30; d <- 970

risk_exposed   <- a / (a + b)
risk_unexposed <- cc / (cc + d)

rr <- risk_exposed / risk_unexposed
round(rr, 2)
```

**RR = 3.00.** Smokers were three times as likely to develop CHD.

How to read any risk ratio:

| RR | Means |
|---|---|
| 1 | no association; the two risks are the same |
| above 1 | exposure is associated with **more** disease |
| below 1 | exposure is associated with **less** disease — protective |

::: {.callout-warning}
## "Three times as likely" is not "three times as many people"
The RR is 3, but the extra risk is 6 people per 100 over five years. A large
ratio on top of a tiny baseline risk is still a tiny absolute effect. This is a
common way health statistics mislead in the press, and it is why the risk
difference below matters as much as the ratio.
:::

## Risk difference — how much extra disease

$$\text{RD} = \text{risk}_{\text{exposed}} - \text{risk}_{\text{unexposed}}$$

```{webr}
a <- 90; b <- 910; cc <- 30; d <- 970

rd <- a / (a + b) - cc / (cc + d)
rd
```

**RD = 0.06**, or 6 extra cases per 100 smokers over five years.

The ratio tells you about **cause**: how strongly is this exposure related to
this disease? The difference tells you about **impact**: how much disease would
go away if the exposure did?

A good results section reports both. A paper reporting only the ratio is often
hiding a small absolute effect.

## Number needed to treat, and to harm

$$\text{NNT} = \frac{1}{|\text{RD}|}$$

```{webr}
a <- 90; b <- 910; cc <- 30; d <- 970

rd  <- a / (a + b) - cc / (cc + d)
nnt <- 1 / abs(rd)
round(nnt, 1)
```

**16.7.** Because the exposure here is harmful, this is a *number needed to
harm*: about 17 people would have to smoke for five years for one extra case of
CHD to appear.

Always round NNT **up** when you report it, and always state the time period.
"NNT 17 over five years" is a sentence a patient can act on. "NNT 17" is not.

## Odds ratio — the one people get wrong

Odds is not risk. Odds compares those with the disease to those **without**,
rather than to the total.

$$\text{odds} = \frac{a}{b} \qquad \text{OR} = \frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{a \times d}{b \times c}$$

```{webr}
a <- 90; b <- 910; cc <- 30; d <- 970

or <- (a * d) / (b * cc)
round(or, 2)
```

**OR = 3.20**, against an RR of 3.00. The odds ratio is further from 1 than the
risk ratio. It always is, when the exposure is harmful.

::: {.callout-note}
## Then why use the odds ratio at all?
Because in a **case-control study you cannot compute a risk.** You chose how
many cases and how many controls to recruit, so `a + b` is a number you decided,
not a number you observed. Any risk you calculate from it is an artefact of your
own sampling.

The odds ratio survives that. It is the same whether you sample on exposure or
on disease, which is exactly why case-control studies work at all. Primer 8 is
about this.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The rare disease assumption
When the disease is rare, `b` is close to `a + b` and `d` is close to `c + d`, so
OR ≈ RR. When the disease is common, they diverge sharply, and an OR read aloud
as "three times more likely" overstates the effect.

Our example has a 9% risk — not rare — and the OR is already 7% higher than the
RR. At 30% risk the gap would be much wider. **Never describe an odds ratio in
the words of a risk ratio unless the outcome is genuinely uncommon.**
:::

## Attributable fraction — how much of the disease is down to this

Among the exposed, what share of their disease is attributable to the exposure?

$$\text{AF}_{\text{exposed}} = \frac{\text{RR} - 1}{\text{RR}}$$

```{webr}
rr <- 3.0

af_exposed <- (rr - 1) / rr
round(af_exposed, 3)
```

**0.667.** Two-thirds of the CHD occurring in smokers is attributable to their
smoking — assuming the association is causal and unconfounded, which is the
assumption Primer 9 takes apart.

For the whole population you also need how common the exposure is:

```{webr}
a <- 90; b <- 910; cc <- 30; d <- 970

risk_total     <- (a + cc) / (a + b + cc + d)
risk_unexposed <- cc / (cc + d)

paf <- (risk_total - risk_unexposed) / risk_total
round(paf, 3)
```

**0.5.** Half of all CHD in this population is attributable to smoking — because
half the population smokes and smoking triples the risk. A strong exposure that
almost nobody has moves this number very little; that is why population impact
and individual risk are different arguments.

## Doing it with a table object

You will usually get a 2×2 out of `table()` rather than by typing four numbers.

```{webr}
# 12 people: exposure and outcome as logical vectors
exposed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE,
             FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
disease <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE,
             TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)

tab <- table(exposed, disease)
tab
```

Read the printed table before you trust it. `table()` sorts its levels
alphabetically, which puts `FALSE` before `TRUE` — so the **first** row is the
unexposed and the **first** column is the non-diseased. That is upside down and
back to front compared with the layout above.

```{webr}
exposed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE,
             FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
disease <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE,
             TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
tab <- table(exposed, disease)

# Pull the cells out by NAME, never by position.
a  <- tab["TRUE",  "TRUE"]
b  <- tab["TRUE",  "FALSE"]
cc <- tab["FALSE", "TRUE"]
d  <- tab["FALSE", "FALSE"]

c(a = a, b = b, cc = cc, d = d)

rr <- (a / (a + b)) / (cc / (cc + d))
round(rr, 2)
```

**RR = 3.00** again: 3 of 6 exposed versus 1 of 6 unexposed.

::: {.callout-important}
## Index by name, not by position
`tab[2, 2]` will silently become the wrong cell the moment your data has a
different set of levels, or a level with no observations in it. `tab["TRUE",
"TRUE"]` either gives the right cell or fails loudly. On the course we use
`epitools`, which handles the ordering for you — but you still have to know
which way round the table is before you trust what it returns.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: risk ratio"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

A cohort study of a water-borne outbreak:

<table class="twobytwo">
<tr><th></th><th>Ill</th><th>Not ill</th><th>Total</th></tr>
<tr><th>Drank tank water</th><td>56</td><td>144</td><td>200</td></tr>
<tr><th>Did not</th><td>18</td><td>282</td><td>300</td></tr>
</table>

Compute the risk ratio, rounded to 2 decimal places.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - ex_rr
#|   - ex_rd
#|   - ex_or
a <- 56    # exposed,   ill
b <- 144   # exposed,   not ill
cc <- 18   # unexposed, ill
d <- 282   # unexposed, not ill
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rr
______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rr
#| solution: true
round((a / (a + b)) / (cc / (cc + d)), 2)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rr
#| check: true
# Risk exposed 56/200 = 0.28.  Risk unexposed 18/300 = 0.06.  RR = 4.6667.
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 4.67))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — RR 4.67. People who drank tank water were about 4.7 times as likely to fall ill.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 3.11, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You divided 56 by 18: that compares the case counts, not the risks. Each group has a different total, so you must turn each into a risk first.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.21, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is upside down: you divided the unexposed risk by the exposed risk. Exposed goes on top.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 6.09, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the odds ratio. A risk uses the group total as its denominator (a + b), not the non-cases (b).")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. Risk in the exposed is a/(a+b); risk in the unexposed is cc/(cc+d); divide the first by the second.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "One number. Work out each group's risk, then divide exposed by unexposed, then round to 2.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_rr"}
Two risks first: 56 out of 200, and 18 out of 300. Then divide the exposed risk
by the unexposed risk.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: risk difference and NNT"}
**Time:** 6 minutes

Same outbreak table. Compute the **risk difference**, rounded to 3 decimal
places.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rd
______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rd
#| solution: true
round(a / (a + b) - cc / (cc + d), 3)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rd
#| check: true
# 0.28 - 0.06 = 0.22
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.22))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 0.22, so 22 extra illnesses per 100 people who drank the water. The reciprocal, 1/0.22, is about 4.5: roughly 5 people had to drink it for one extra illness.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), -0.22))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right size, wrong sign. Exposed minus unexposed, in that order.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 4.667, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the risk ratio. A difference subtracts; a ratio divides.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. Subtract the unexposed risk from the exposed risk.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "One number: a/(a+b) minus cc/(cc+d), rounded to 3 places.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_rd"}
Same two risks as the last exercise. This time subtract instead of dividing.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3: odds ratio"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Same table again. Compute the **odds ratio**, rounded to 2 decimal places, then
compare it with the risk ratio of 4.67.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_or
______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_or
#| solution: true
round((a * d) / (b * cc), 2)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_or
#| check: true
# (56*282) / (144*18) = 15792 / 2592 = 6.0926
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 6.09))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — OR 6.09 against an RR of 4.67. The outcome here is common (28% in the exposed), so the odds ratio badly overstates the risk ratio. Do not read this one aloud as 'six times more likely'.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 4.67, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the risk ratio again. Odds uses b and d as denominators, not the group totals.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.16, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the reciprocal: you have b*cc on top. The cross product is a*d over b*cc.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. The cross product is (a * d) / (b * cc).")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "One number: (a * d) / (b * cc), rounded to 2 places.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_or"}
The odds ratio is the cross product: multiply the two diagonal cells that
contain `a` and `d`, and divide by the product of the other two.
:::
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Lay out a 2×2 table the same way every time, exposure down the side.
- Compute a risk ratio, a risk difference, an odds ratio and an NNT from it.
- Say what each one is for: ratio for cause, difference for impact.
- Explain why an odds ratio is not a risk ratio, and when the gap matters.
- Compute an attributable fraction, and say what it assumes.
- Pull cells out of a `table()` by name rather than by position.

::: {.callout-important}
## Everything on this page assumes the comparison is fair
Every measure here compares exposed with unexposed as if those two groups
differed *only* in the exposure. They almost never do. That is Primer 9, and it
is the one that changes how you read papers.
:::

→ [**Primer 8: study designs**](primer-epi-03-designs.qmd)
